title: Snowball Earth, When Ice Reached the Equator
description: Tonight is about a winter that lasted tens of millions of years. By the strongest reading of the evidence, twice, for millions of years at a stretch, ice reached the equator and a great deal of the ocean lay under it. And as far as anyone can currently show, nothing with a nervous system was alive to notice. The cast is microbes, algae, stone and ice, and the slow weather of a very long time.

It is told through what the stone kept: stones dropped into fine mud by melting ice, magnetism in old rock that puts glaciers near the equator, and a pale carbonate rock laid over the ice's debris on many continents. It is also, quietly, a story about the thaw, and about a warm sea afterwards.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. Whether the ocean was ever sealed from pole to pole is still argued between careful people, and the episode gives both sides their best case. What set the first freeze off is a leading idea, not a settled answer. How fast the thaw came, how long the pale rock took to form, and whether anything like an animal was already here are all open. Where researchers disagree, it says so.
It stays gentle throughout: nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and it ends on the far side of the ice.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the ice melts, that's the intended use.

accuracy: Every factual claim traces to a named, published source, listed below. Snowball Earth is a well-supported idea with real, ongoing disputes, and where the sources disagree the episode gives the range rather than the tidier answer. Some sources were checked at abstract level.

sources.title: The World Before the Ice, and Why It Ran Away

sources.cite: Macdonald & Swanson-Hysell (2023), Elements - Rodinia's breakup and the Franklin volcanic province
Pierrehumbert et al. (2011), Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences - a Sun about 94% as bright as today's
Hoffman et al. (2017), Science Advances - the main review: ice-albedo feedback, durations, the thaw
Rooney et al. (2014), PNAS; Macdonald et al. (2010), Science - dating the first glaciation
Prave et al. (2016), Geology; Tasistro-Hart et al. (2025), PNAS - the second glaciation, at least about four million years
Sohl, Christie-Blick & Kent (1999), GSA Bulletin; Evans & Raub (2011), Geol. Soc. Memoir 36 - magnetism puts glacial rock at low latitudes
Hoffman & Schrag (2002), Terra Nova - dropstones, striated stones, the case for a snowball
Cox et al. (2013), Chemical Geology - iron-rich layers of the first glaciation
Hoffman et al. (2017); Husain et al. (2025), Nature Communications - meltwater ponds, with a living modern comparison
Nettersheim et al. (2019); Bobrovskiy et al. (2021), both Nature Ecol. & Evol. - the disputed sponge biomarkers
Brocks et al. (2017), Nature - algae rise between the glaciations
